1:
The warning against suretyship gets its setting from Charles Ellicott, who explains why the practice existed at all. When the law was given, he says, the people had not taken up commerce, and the only occasion for a loan was to supply the borrower’s immediate necessities, so that exacting interest would have produced great hardship, the insolvent debtor and his family becoming the creditor’s slaves; lending on interest to a poor Israelite was therefore forbidden and the people enjoined to lend for nothing. But by the time of Solomon commerce had developed enormously, communications were opened with Spain and Egypt and possibly India and Ceylon while caravans went beyond the Euphrates, and lending on interest for trade became frequent, and with it suretyship, the pledging of a man’s credit for his friend. John Wesley reaches the same institution from the other side, that the creditor is called a stranger because the usurers of that nation were heathens or reputed as bad, the practice being forbidden; and he enters the one qualification the chapter needs, that suretyship may in some cases be an act of justice and charity, the warning being against doing it rashly.

Matthew Henry begins higher up, with the praise of a book that teaches not only divine wisdom for another world but human prudence for this; and he grades the danger, since it is hazardous enough to be bound for a friend whose circumstances one knows and much more to strike hands with a stranger, though the stranger may be the creditor, to whom a man becomes bound although he owes him nothing. Adam Clarke describes what the arrangement does to the other man: the burden is taken off his shoulders and laid on yours, and knowing that someone stands between him and the demands of law he feels little responsibility, his spirit of exertion is crippled, and listlessness follows; and the very person for whom the burden was borne may treat his friend with neglect and avoid his presence, lest the pledge be reclaimed.

On the remedy they agree that it must be violent and immediate. Ellicott renders the counsel literally, that a man is to let himself be trampled on and humbly sue, the second verb meaning to assail impetuously and importune. Clarke says the debtor is to be pressed for payment and given no rest, or the surety may expect to be left to pay it. Wesley makes it winning him by incessant and earnest solicitation. John Gill takes the sleeplessness as a measure of what is at stake, since such a man should leave no stone unturned nor method untried to extricate himself.

The last verse turns on two words. Keil and Delitzsch ask first whether the preposition in the first verse introduces the man for whom or the man with whom one becomes surety, and refuse at the fifth to render the bare phrase there as immediately, since that sense is rabbinic and not biblical; Gill takes it in exactly that sense, noting that it sometimes means out of hand with the Jewish writers. They add that the versions translate as though the word were out of the snare, that one scholar prefers that reading and another supposes a word for hunter to have dropped out, and they answer with an objection of their own, that this cannot be the parallelism proposed since a bird-catcher is not at the same time a hunter of gazelles; their own accentuation makes it, tear thyself free like the gazelle from the hand into which thou hast fallen. They derive the one animal’s name from its elegance and the other’s from its whistling. Ellicott notes only that some phrase such as the hand that held him must be supplied; Clarke keeps the image, that a man caught in the snare should make every struggle as the antelope and the bird do.
6:
The ant is sent to as a schoolmaster, and one of them says so. Matthew Henry observes that sluggards must be schooled, and that the teacher has had to find a school low enough for a pupil who will not come to him, since dreaming scholars never love wakeful teachers; man, taught more than the beasts of the earth, is so degenerated that he may learn wisdom from the meanest insects and be shamed by them. Keil and Delitzsch make the same point from another book, where God is said to have set the beasts for our teachers, and add that the creature’s name in their own tongue comes from its industry and in Hebrew from a root for the low, secret motion by which it works.

Adam Clarke answers with natural history, and corrects what the proverb seems to say. The ant is remarkable for foresight and economy, he grants, and no insect is more laborious, not even the bee; but it does not gather in summer against the winter, since it sleeps through the winter and does not eat, so that such a hoard would be useless: it collects when its food is most plentiful, for consumption in the proper season. He adds what he has watched it do with its young, carrying them out, in the state in which they look like a grain of rice, to lie in the sun, and on the approach of rain bringing them in and covering the entrance with a thin stone. John Gill answers with authorities, a philosopher for the ant having no ruler and the naturalists for its working even by moonlight.

The three officers it does without are pressed by the grammarians. Keil and Delitzsch take them for the highest judiciary, police and executive powers, deriving the first from a root meaning to distinguish and the second from one meaning to draw lines or write, and report that two versions confused the first with the word for harvest. Charles Ellicott settles the first, that it properly means judge, then leader or prince. Keil and Delitzsch also distinguish the two seasons of the eighth verse, the late summer when the heat rises highest and the end of harvest, so that the first line shows persevering industry and the second the bringing home of the winter store; they also mention the Aramaic fable of the ant and the grasshopper. Gill has her toiling night and day while the season lasts, knowing nothing is to be got afterwards.

At the sluggard’s own words the commentary turns dramatic. Keil and Delitzsch insist that the tenth verse is not an ironical permission to sleep on but the sluggard’s own reply, spoken to turn away an unwelcome disturber, its diminutives sounding like self-delusion. Gill hears the same voice and traces its gradation: first a few sound sleeps, then, if those cannot be had, a few slumbers to get thoroughly awake, and if not those, at least the folding of the hands. The poverty that follows is read for its pace. Ellicott notes that the form of the word is intensive, one who moves swiftly, used elsewhere of moving on the wings of the wind, so that poverty comes on apace while the sluggard sleeps, and that the armed man is one against whom the sleeper will be defenceless; these two verses, he adds, are repeated later in the book. Clarke takes the traveller the other way, as coming with slow but surely approaching steps while the want comes with irresistible fury, and reports that three versions and an old English one add a further clause, that if thou wilt be diligent thy harvest shall be as a fountain and poverty shall flee far from thee. Gill allows both paces, swiftly like a traveller arriving unawares, or by slow steps but surely. John Wesley settles it in four words: swiftly and unexpectedly, irresistibly.
12:
The man of Belial is named rather than described, and the name detains them. Matthew Henry would have had the phrase left untranslated, since the term is often used in Scripture, and takes the man for one who makes a trade of doing evil, especially with his tongue. John Gill divides the two words, the first meaning an unprofitable man, good for nothing, or else one lawless who has thrown off the yoke, Belial being a name of the devil; and he ends where he often ends, with the man of sin. Adam Clarke renders it good for nothing and refers it to the first man when he lost his innocence, whose posterity, unless restored by grace, are sinners by trade. Charles Ellicott gives the original meaning in a word, worthless; Keil and Delitzsch ask instead which part of the sentence is subject and which predicate.

The signs he makes occasion the chapter’s most curious note. Clarke holds that these things are spoken of debauchees, and quotes a Latin elegy in which a lover instructs his mistress how to signal to him at a banquet, by touching his foot, by speaking with the eyebrows, by tracing words in spilt wine; the whole is in the same strain, he says, and though it has been translated it cannot be introduced here. Ellicott sees another figure, a malicious tattler who fills out his lying tale with winks, so that more is suggested than said, to the blasting of his neighbour’s character. Keil and Delitzsch spend their space on the verb, which does not properly mean winking, since it is used of the lips as well as the eyes, but unites the senses of pinching with a sharp instrument and with a blunt one, and so means to nip the eyes together. Gill keeps to the manner, the air of a sneering man who winks at another’s weakness in company. At the sowing of discord Keil and Delitzsch prefer one classical figure to another, the unfettering of the winds by Aeolus rather than the casting in of the apple; Clarke makes the discord domestic, sown between men and their wives.

The suddenness of the ruin is illustrated three ways. Keil and Delitzsch take the verb of the brittle potter’s vessel, a frequent figure for the destruction of an army, a city or a man. Ellicott uses the same figure and adds a judgment: this character seems especially hateful to God, being described in like terms in a psalm and held up in the next verses as the worst of the seven things named. Clarke guesses at a particular punishment, that the breaking may allude to stoning, a multitude joining to overwhelm the man. Gill keeps it general, that he who devises mischief secretly gets no warning of his ruin.

The list that follows is a form with a name, and two of them give it. Ellicott calls the shape a climax, six things hated and the seventh worse than all, reports the term later writers give such numerical proverbs, and observes that wherever the form occurs the number first named is afterwards increased by one, a peculiarity absent from three other instances. Keil and Delitzsch use the same term and draw the point of the climax, that no vice is a greater abomination to God than the striving to set at variance men who love one another. Clarke goes through the seven with a gloss on each: the exalted eyes of those who will not condescend to look on the rest of mankind, the hands that shed innocent blood by murder or by battery, and last the man who troubles the peace of a family, a village or a state. Gill notes that pride stands first as probably the first sin committed, of the angels and of the first man; John Wesley glosses the swift feet as those who greedily execute their designs.
20:
The return to the father’s commandment is marked as a return. Keil and Delitzsch observe that after three shorter sections the teacher comes back to the theme of an earlier one, the warning against sins of the flesh, whose consequences cannot sufficiently be held before the young; they note that the figure of binding recalls the phylactery and the amulet. Adam Clarke refers back to earlier chapters for the commandment and the binding, adding that the allusion is to the command about writing the words on the hand and doorpost. John Gill is careful about the persons: the words are not the father’s to the son of an earlier chapter but the writer’s own, addressed to everyone who came to him for instruction and to everyone standing in that relation to a religious father, the commandment being no other than God’s as pious parents teach it. John Wesley puts it in seven words, the word of God delivered by thy parents.

When the teaching is said to lead and watch and talk, the personification is noticed by two. Keil and Delitzsch say the good doctrine is here personified and identified with wisdom herself, that the verbs are promises and not wishes, and that the three circumstances distinguished, going, lying down and rising up, follow the order of an older formula. Clarke makes the figure domestic: the law is a nurse, a teacher and a guardian by night and day, so that an upright man never goes but as the word directs, commends body and soul to his Maker when he lies down, and wakes to the promises of God. Gill keeps to the leading, that the law directs a man what way to shun and which to walk in.

The lamp and the light are distinguished by the grammarians and applied by the rest. Keil and Delitzsch make them general and particular: the instruction is light, which enlightens the man who submits to it, and the commandment a lamp kindled at that light, enlightening the darkness of ignorance about conduct; they add that the word for instruction here has not its specifically national sense but the general one of teaching about the will of God. Charles Ellicott turns the distinction into counsel for a man in perplexity: darkness may seem to have settled on his path, but there is always some command he cannot doubt, some instruction offering itself as a guide, some discipline that tells him what to shun; and by following the duty he knows he prepares himself for more light, so that his path shines more and more. Clarke states it plainly, that the commandment illuminates our path and the law shows the will of God, while the reproofs that rebuke our errors lead us into the way of life. Matthew Henry divides it another way, that by its arguments the word is a light to which our understanding must subscribe and by its authority a law to which our will must submit; no such light ever shone from the schools of the philosophers, and no law so well framed ever issued from the throne of a prince.

At the purpose of the instruction, to keep a man from the evil woman, Clarke turns personal, remarking that the writer had suffered sorely from that quarter, which is why the cautions are repeated; and he defines the term, that the strange woman always means one not a man’s own and may also mean a foreigner, a stranger to the God of that nation. Keil and Delitzsch work on the second clause and reject the rendering, adopted by two scholars and two old Greek versions, which makes it the smooth-tongued foreign woman, since the noun is not an adjective and the anomaly assumed is unnecessary. Gill draws the practical link, that the law directs to duties which require diligence and so prevent idleness, that inlet to all sin.
25:
The eyelids that catch a man are explained from the toilet table. Adam Clarke reports that painting the eyelids is a general custom in the East, of which he has many Asiatic drawings, and that antimony polishes the eyes so that they take an indescribable lustre, one observer writing that they appear to be swimming in bliss. Keil and Delitzsch set the first clause beside the tenth commandment and the sentence of the Sermon on the Mount about the heart, and cite a Talmudic saying that the imagination of a sinful act exhausts the body even more than the act itself. John Gill distinguishes the eye from the thought, the one kindling lust in the heart and the other cherishing it into flame.

The piece of bread is where the versions part. Clarke reports that the Greek gives the clause a strange turn, making the hire of a harlot about one loaf, so many were such women in the land that they hired themselves for a bare subsistence, and that three other versions follow it; the sense, he thinks, is that while the man hires for a loaf the woman takes his life, extracting his energy and poisoning his constitution. Gill keeps the received reading and applies it to the man, brought so low that he must beg a morsel, as the prodigal did who envied the swine their husks.

The two questions about fire are agreed to be proverbial, and two cite the same philosopher. Clarke says only that these were proverbial expressions plain to every capacity. Gill notes that a whore is compared to fire by the poets and quotes a Greek sage; Keil and Delitzsch quote the same sage, that to fall into fire and into a woman come to the same thing, and add that the verb for burning is the one that leaves a brand-mark, and that the phrases of the next verse are euphemisms.

The comparison with the thief is where the chapter argues rather than warns. Keil and Delitzsch set the two side by side so that adultery appears the greater crime, and dispute the usual explanation of the first clause, since the verb has there been given a sense devised for this passage alone. Charles Ellicott puts it in two sentences: a man driven to theft by poverty is more worthy of pity than disdain, but not the adulterer; and the thief can make retribution, while the adulterer has none to offer. Clarke agrees that everyone pities the culprit who stole for hunger, but adds that no law clears him, since he must make restitution and be sold as a bondsman if he cannot pay. On the sevenfold restitution Gill canvasses three explanations, a Jewish authority who reaches the number by adding the double and the fivefold of the law, others who suppose a foreign law or a penalty increased later, and his own preference, that it means perfect restitution as often as he is found guilty. Ellicott reads the clause as permission rather than requirement, that he may restore sevenfold and give up all the wealth of his house, the law having required less. John Wesley makes it not the restitution the law required but what the wronged man might exact or the thief would give rather than be exposed to public shame.

At the injured husband the chapter closes without mercy. Keil and Delitzsch state the principle, that one who has been stolen from may be appeased but not the injured husband, and explain the jealousy as the glow of a man’s anger put forth with all his strength. Clarke supplies a Roman punishment inflicted by such husbands, so disgraceful that it commonly caused the offender’s death; Gill offers three sources for the wound, the husband, the magistrate, or diseases sent by God, and observes that men who do not despise a thief will despise an adulterer.
